    Taylor Series

    Studying power series is largely for the purpose of Taylor series.

    From the crossing of infinitely differentiable and analytic

    If a function satisfies in the neighborhood of (i.e., infinitely differentiable), we can always formally construct an infinite series based on the Taylor formula:

    This series is called the Taylor series (it is the Maclaurin series when ). Since the Taylor series is essentially a power series, as long as it converges in some interval , its coefficients are uniquely determined by its successive derivatives: .

    However, calculus leaves an intuitive trap here. Generally, even if the Taylor series converges perfectly in an interval, it is not guaranteed to converge to the original function itself. In other words, is not obvious. To see the underlying nature, we need to broaden our view from the isolated real axis to the two-dimensional complex plane.

    The “Hidden Reef” on the Imaginary Axis: The Geometric Nature of the Radius of Convergence

    Consider two functions that behave completely differently on the real axis, yet their Maclaurin series exhibit a symmetrical limitation:

    1. The Natural Boundary of the Geometric Series

    The radius of convergence of this series is . In the real domain, this limitation is very intuitive: when , the denominator of the function becomes zero, creating an “singularity” in the analytic construction.

    2. The Mysterious Restriction of the Arctangent Function

    On the real axis, is an impeccable perfect function—it is not only continuous everywhere but also infinitely differentiable, with no points where the denominator is zero. However, its Taylor series radius of convergence is also strictly limited to . If we only look at the real axis, this is undoubtedly a puzzling mystery.

    When we introduce complex numbers and perform analytic continuation of the function using the complex logarithm form, the truth emerges:

    On the complex plane, the complex arctangent function has a zero denominator at . The singularity in the complex plane limits the radius of convergence in the real domain.

    Geometrically, the region of convergence for a power series in the complex plane is a circle. The boundary of this circle must touch the singularity closest to the origin. The distance of these two singularities, hidden on the imaginary axis , from the origin is exactly 1, thus defining a circle of radius 1. The interval of convergence we see on the real axis is merely a projection of this complex plane convergence circle onto the real axis.

    The False Docility: The Bipolar Nature of Pathological Functions in Real and Complex Domains

    To completely draw the line between “infinitely differentiable” and “analytic,” we need to examine the famous pathological function in mathematical analysis:

    This function is extremely peculiar on the real axis. If you compute its derivatives of all orders at the origin , you will find that due to the suppression from the exponentially decaying terms, every derivative of any order at the origin is exactly 0 (). This means its Maclaurin series becomes the trivial series that is identically zero:

    This series clearly converges on the entire real axis, but except at this point, it is not equal to the original function anywhere .

    This “docility” on the real axis deceives us. Once the function is extended to the complex plane , approaching the origin from different directions, it exhibits a completely opposite dynamic:

    • Approaching along the real axis ():

    The function value smoothly slides towards zero, and the derivatives of all orders are silent.

    • Approaching along the imaginary axis ():

    As approaches the origin, the function value undergoes a violent exponential explosion.

    The origin is actually an essential singularity of the function in the complex plane. Its infinite smoothness on the real axis is merely an illusion left behind by the violent dynamics in the complex plane projected onto the real axis. This ultimately explains why its Taylor series can never truly represent the function itself. For a real function to be perfectly locally approximated by a Taylor series (i.e., to be analytic), it must not only be smooth on the real axis but must also withstand the test of approximation from all directions in the complex plane.

    The Remainder Term of the Taylor Formula and the Determination of Series Convergence

    Since we are further refining our study, moving from power series to Taylor series, we naturally have better properties, and here we use the remainder term to determine the convergence of the series.

    When studying the Taylor expansion of a function, in order to precisely measure the approximation error between the finite-order Taylor polynomial and the original function , the concept of the Remainder Term was introduced:

    Depending on the application scenario (error estimation or convergence proof), there are two classic quantitative forms for the remainder term.

    Two Classic Forms of the Taylor Remainder Term

    Assume that the function has derivatives up to the order in the interval containing and , then the remainder term can be expressed as:

    Where . This form can be seen as a higher-order generalization of the Lagrange Mean Value Theorem and is very suitable for estimating the upper bound of the function value error.

    2. Cauchy Form of the Remainder Term

    Where . The Cauchy remainder term is more powerful in proving the convergence of certain special functions (such as or ) when approaching the convergence boundary.

    Left boundary: Substitute the term into the series, and the general term becomes .

    At first glance, the introduction of signs seems to complicate matters, but if you extend your gaze to infinity (when ), you will find that the ratio of adjacent terms is quietly and constantly positive. This means that, in the vast expanse far from the origin, it actually transforms into a series of the same sign.

    Faced with this seemingly gentle but lacking cancellation mechanism of same-sign term accumulation, we need to invoke Raabe’s Test—a fine tool specifically designed to quantitatively measure the rate of decay of a series by magnifying higher-order small terms when the ratio test fails. Let’s capture its limit behavior:

    Raabe’s Test is very objective: the series converges if the limit value is greater than 1, and diverges if it is less than 1.

    • When , that is , the rate of decay is fast enough, and the series converges.

    • When , that is , the momentum of accumulation overcomes the decay, and the series diverges.

    (Note: When , the function degenerates to the constant 1, and the series naturally converges trivially, so it is generally not discussed as a pathological case.)

    Right boundary: When the gaze turns to the right side, the general term becomes .

    Conversely, when is large enough, . The signs here begin to oscillate regularly like a pendulum, and the series becomes a standard long-range alternating series.

    Alternating series often possess a tolerance protection granted by ‘positive-negative cancellation.’ Even if the sum of the absolute values tends to infinity, as long as the wave of positive and negative alternates uniformly enough, they can reach a truce in the dynamic:

    • : From the previous Raabe’s Test, we know that even its absolute sum converges at this point, so it naturally converges.

    • : Although the shield of absolute values is shattered, the sword of alternating cancellation remains. With the fine scrutiny of the Leibniz Test, the magnitude of the terms still monotonically approaches 0, allowing the series to maintain a fragile balance, exhibiting conditional convergence—meaning the series itself lives on by positive and negative cancellation, but collapses once the signs are removed and absolute values are taken.

    • : At this point, the dangerous threshold is crossed, and the general term cannot even maintain the basic baseline of ‘approaching zero’ as it tends to infinity; the amplitude of the positive and negative oscillations grows larger and larger, and the series completely diverges.
